b053278f32e7d7f5: The longest a human being has lived is 122 years while the average global life expectancy is 74 years.
Malaysia's is 74 to 77 years, the oldest ever recorded is 113 years. In striving for a long life, the salutation "semoga panjang umur" (may you live long) is imbued in prayers and birthday wishes.
The real objective is good mental and physical health, and reliable financial means for sustenance, medical emergencies and leisurely pursuits.
The concern was expressed by Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah, who affirmed that healthy ageing should not be a privilege reserved only for those who can afford it.
In delivering his royal address at a wellness forum, the Sultan of Perak asserted that healthy ageing must be inclusive, accessible through environment, services and technology.

Sultan Nazrin has compelled us to do a rethink on what it means to live longer. We must reconfigure retirement and pension systems, lifetime education, employment opportunities, healthcare financing, wealth distribution and inter-generational wealth transfers.
It doesn't just mean avoiding illness or maintaining a strong physique: it also means an active, meaningful and independent life for the duration of our lives.
Malaysia is on the right path with the National Policy for Older Persons: elderly and preventive healthcare, senior citizen centres and chronic disease management.
In doing so, the plan is to combat ageism and discrimination, create age-friendly communities, provide integrated and long-term healthcare.
As leading examples, healthy ageing in Japan and Singapore are national priorities, something Malaysia is inadequately prepared for.

Here's what is needed: a national strategy combining retirement income, health and long-term care, housing and social protection because in 2036, Malaysia becomes an ageing nation when 15 per cent of the population is 60 and above.
With more people retiring, medical services spike and the elderly need extra help with daily activities. Pension and retirement savings will face increasing pressure.
For now, only 15 per cent of seniors age healthily, based on daily routine, cognitive health, social support and absence of chronic diseases.
Malaysia may need investments of RM10 to RM15 billion annually to establish a comprehensive national healthy-ageing programme until 2031.
Funding goes to demands for elderly care, trained caregivers and affordable long-term care facilities on top of equitable access to rural communities and lower-income families.
Employers, local authorities, communities and families have to step up with practical policies, adequate funding and accessible services.
We can't wait for the aged nation fallout: healthy ageing is not measured by longevity but by the quality of our remaining years.
ab20d5e7cc8b35c1: Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone.
The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update.

Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned.

Support for Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended on October 14, 2025, but the company announced an Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in July 2025. The plan was that this program would end on April 14, 2026, by which time customers would surely have made the jump to a later or online version, right? The company said: "This period will not be extended past April 2026 (you do not need to ask)."

And... of course it was. As April 2026 rolled around, and it became clear that some customers were still stubbornly sticking with the old versions, Microsoft did the equivalent of heaving an exasperated sigh and offered another six months of paid security updates. Those final weeks also brought a separate treat: a Windows Server update breaking Exchange Server.
This time it was serious. Microsoft released the final Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 security updates on October 13. No more patches, no more vulnerability testing, and apparently no more reprieves.

According to Microsoft's Security Update Guide, the November update fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server SE, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft isn't testing earlier versions of Exchange for the vulnerabilities. ®
c9bbd542b160813e: KUALA LUMPUR: Police will send officers to Pakistan to investigate the detention of 130 Malaysians in a raid on a suspected scam centre in Rawalpindi last month.
Commercial Crime Investigation Department (CCID) director Datuk Rusdi Mohd Isa said the officers would meet Pakistani authorities, record statements and examine devices seized during the raid.
He said examining the evidence was important to uncover the syndicate's modus operandi, including its alleged use of Royal Malaysia Police uniforms to deceive victims.

"We need to arrange a meeting to obtain statements from the authorities there, as well as examine the evidence and devices seized. We also want more information about the parties who brought them to Pakistan," he said at the CCID monthly press conference at Bukit Aman.

Rusdi said police received information about the detention at the end of October through official channels involving the Home Ministry and their Pakistani counterparts, although the arrests were made on Oct 13.
The identities of all 130 Malaysians were subsequently confirmed through cooperation between the police, embassies and Interpol.

He said 59 of those detained were from Sabah and 57 from Sarawak, with the rest from Johor, Selangor, Kuala Lumpur and Kelantan. Checks found that 92 had no criminal records in Malaysia, while the others had records involving various offences, including drugs, fraud and gambling. Two were wanted in connection with fraud cases in Sabah.

On their immigration status, 107 had overstayed their visas, 20 had valid visas, two had visa extensions and one had no valid travel documents. The Malaysians arrived in Pakistan in stages between June 8 and Sept 29, with the highest number, 53, arriving on Aug 3.

Addressing claims that they had been deceived by job offers, Rusdi said investigative experience showed that some people taken overseas to work for scam syndicates might have known the real purpose of their recruitment.

"However, based on investigative experience, there are individuals who are believed to know the true purpose of being taken abroad to work for a scam syndicate, but play different roles such as call operators, cooks or supervisors," he said.

Pakistani media previously reported that the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency raided premises at Kasa Tower, Bahria Town Phase VIII, Rawalpindi, allegedly used as a call centre for financial scams targeting Malaysians.
The syndicate reportedly impersonated bank customer service officers and police, using false allegations of money laundering to deceive victims. -- BERNAMA
f98f612fda85d6f2: Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. 3ea0223e76944cc2: MOSCOW: Vladimir Putin indicated Thursday that Russia will not compromise on its hardline demands to end the Ukraine offensive, but offered a short-term ceasefire in a key frontline city during a Kremlin meeting with US envoys.

The Russian president said he would not water down his territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine that Russia claims to have annexed, and ruled out agreeing to foreign peacekeeping troops being stationed in Ukraine -- a deployment that he said would be a "continuation of war".
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were in Moscow after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi searching for a way to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II.

Putin's comments appeared to douse hopes that a deal to end the war could be within grasp, after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said there was a "window of opportunity" to achieve "a result" before 2027.
The Americans, meanwhile, urged Putin to allow European representatives to sit at the table for the next round of talks.
Moscow has successfully managed to reframe the discussions on the war as part of a wider discussion about European security.

But Kyiv and European leaders have urged against a new "Yalta" -- a reference to the post-WWII deal to carve the continent into spheres of influence -- and said talks must be focused on ending the Ukraine war first.
Kushner and Witkoff will travel to Dublin, where a European summit is taking place, to meet Zelensky later on Thursday.
'Continuation of war'
Usually held behind closed doors, the Kremlin chose to televise a lengthy opening exchange between Putin and the US envoys.
The Russian leader rejected talk of a possible territorial settlement involving "grey" -- or demilitarised -- zones between Ukrainian and Russian positions.
"For us, there is only one line of demarcation: the state border. Because then it will be clear and obvious: here are we, and here are you," he said.

Russia has seized swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine since launching its full-scale offensive in 2022. That is in addition to Crimea, which it annexed in 2014, and territory that was under the control of Russian-backed separatists.
Moscow has formally annexed four regions of Ukraine -- Donetsk, Kherson, Lugansk and Zaporizhzhia -- despite not having full control over them.
The annexations are rejected by Kyiv and the West as illegal and not recognised by the international community.
Advances by Russia's army have slowed throughout 2026 and hundreds of thousands have been killed in the almost five-year conflict, with millions more forced to flee their homes.
Putin proposed organising what he called a "humanitarian mission" to the frontline city of Kostyantynivka, where he said some 400-500 civilians still lived.
Russia claimed in the summer to have captured the city, but Ukraine insists fighting is ongoing for control.
The idea would be modelled on a short-term truce that last month allowed hundreds of stranded and starving locals to flee the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
Putin also repeated his long-standing objection to any foreign troops being deployed to Ukraine as a post-war peacekeeping force -- something Kyiv says is crucial to thwarting another Russian attack.
Moscow would see any foreign troops deployed in the country as a "legitimate target," Putin said, adding their deployment would be a "vicious circle" and mean "the continuation of war".
'United vision'
European countries have been rattled by Russia pushing a review of the entire continent's security architecture, with the US also floating a new framework.
That is widely seen as a reference to Moscow's long-standing demands to push back the Nato military alliance in eastern Europe and end Western military support to Kyiv.

Some 50 European leaders gathered in the Irish capital Thursday, where EU chief Antonio Costa said "there is no need to reinvent the wheel" on Europe's security framework as he accused Russia of wrecking it by attacking Ukraine.
French president Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Europe to rally behind a "clear and united vision" on what it wants from Ukraine talks.
Russia and the US are pushing Europe to name a single representative who they can deal with.
Amid the talks, the death and destruction continued.
Overnight, Russian strikes hit a residential building in Kyiv, killing one person.
In Putin's home city of Saint Petersburg, a car bomb blast killed a Russian soldier -- the latest in a string of apparent assassinations of military figures inside Russia.
Zelensky also reported fresh restrictions had been placed on the Starshield satellite internet service, key to Ukraine's front line communications.
8b65f0d9b5de306d: MELAKA TENGAH: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has rejected claims that he defied the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim in the government’s handling of former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest, insisting that his relationship with the king remains cordial.
Speaking at an event in Ayer Molek here tonight, Anwar said the king had personally called him this evening and he dismissed allegations that his relationship with the palace had deteriorated.
Anwar said the house arrest issue was not within his power to decide unilaterally, but had to be resolved through the relevant judicial processes.
“They say I have defied the Yang di-Pertuan Agong. The Yang di-Pertuan Agong called me this evening. Our relationship is good.
“His Majesty saw that Najib had spent four long years in prison and wanted him to be placed under house arrest. That was not within my power. My powers are determined by the law,” he said.

Anwar said the attorney-general was responsible for ensuring that every government decision and action complied with the law, including seeking clarification and referring the matter to the court for a ruling.
“The attorney-general took time because he is responsible for upholding the law. His Majesty ordered (Najib's house arrest), and the attorney-general said yes.
“We followed the process and had to bring the matter to court to determine when it could be implemented. That's all,” he said.

Najib, 73, arrived at his home in Jalan Langgak Duta, Taman Duta, on Tuesday night to serve the remainder of his six-year prison sentence in the SRC International case, having previously been in Kajang prison since Aug 23, 2022.

His 12-year prison sentence was halved in January 2024 under a royal pardon by the then Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah, who also reduced Najib's RM210 million fine to RM50 million.
In September 2026, the current Yang di-Pertuan Agong granted Najib a further conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.
Umno subsequently paid the RM50 million fine using funds raised through a public crowdfunding exercise.
Separately, Anwar said an Umno minister had expressed doubt about the government’s ability to lower fuel prices.

“He sat in a Cabinet meeting and asked if it was even possible to lower fuel prices so much and whether we had the money. Then he came here to Melaka and criticised us. We have lowered the price of RON95 fuel to RM1.99 per litre,” he said.

de3503437db7ad7f: SHAH ALAM: A former director of Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia's (UKM) UKMShape has been charged with 21 counts of money laundering involving more than RM1.55 million.

The underlying offence is linked to Section 23(1) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) Act 2009.
All 21 money-laundering charges were brought under Section 4(1)(b) of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 (AMLATFPUAA).
Deputy public prosecutor Muaz Ahmad Khairuddin conducted the prosecution, while Husin was represented by lawyer Adam Danial.

3e900f340b949d69: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the company, following the revelation of his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and reports of a relationship with another woman who was a company employee.

In a Form 8-K [PDF] filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the GPU maker disclosed that it accepted the resignation of Huang, whom it identified as Jen-Hsun Huang, on November 11, effective immediately.
He is being replaced by chief financial officer Colette Kress, who will serve as interim leader while the board conducts a search for a new CEO.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as president, CEO, and a member of the board of directors ever since, led the GPU maker to become one of the most valuable companies in the world, hitting a hit peak of over $5.5 trillion earlier this year.

His position became untenable following an investigation by the company's board after he admitted to an affair, amid allegations he had a romantic relationship with a woman the US authorities suspected as a Chinese spy.

Reports later surfaced this week of a second alleged affair with an employee of the company itself, reported by the New York Times as being with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care.
A two-week downfall

News of the scandal first broke barely a couple of weeks ago, on October 29, when claims surfaced that Huang had been the target of an espionage plot involving a Chinese businesswoman working for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed which was a customer of Nvidia.

According to the New York Times, US intelligence had reason to believe the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to gather information about Nvidia and its operations for the Beijing government. Megaspeed also faces claims it was illicitly shipping Nvidia products to China, in violation of US export controls.

Any relationship between Huang and a Chinese operative would be enormously concerning, as the US has been trying to keep advanced technology for AI out of the hands of the country, allegedly for security reasons, fearing it might be used for military purposes.
For its part, Beijing rejects the spying allegations, saying they are part of a smear campaign against China.

Shortly after Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating Huang, he sent an email to Nvidia staff apologizing and confessing to having an affair, though he did not explicitly name Alice Huang in his public apology.

It seemed like the leather-jacketed leader might just hang on, since it was difficult to imagine anyone other than him leading the company after all this time. But Nvidia’s shares fell 4.3 percent on November 9 and a further 5.5 percent the following day, wiping around $430 billion off its market value, amid all the speculation.
Then the claim emerged regarding a second affair, with an employee at Nvidia who reported to him, and many commentators took it as a sign the game was up. Huang resigned the same day the news broke.
Indecision ahead

Now the speculation starts over who will take over the reins at Nvidia, but Huang could prove a tough act to follow. He is said to have recognized early on the potential for taking the number-crunching capabilities of graphics processors and putting them to use at accelerating AI processing, and Nvidia’s position today as the leading AI hardware firm is thanks to that bet.

“The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker, Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” says Forrester VP and group research director Stephanie Balaouras.

If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience, she adds. But if its stock or financing relationships remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragility of the AI bubble.

“In the near term, the board did the sensible thing and reached for a steward. Colette Kress knows every number in that order book,” commented Mark Malek, CIO at financial services firm Siebert Financial.

“It does NOT settle the stock. Interim means the real decision is still ahead, the investigations are still open, and next week’s earnings call just became the most important in the company’s history,” he added. ®

8cf6a24e025ce1a2: PAPAR: A husband and wife were found dead in a sewage pond at a pig farm in Kampung Kawari, Papar.
They were found in an embrace. Police believe the 52-year-old man slipped into the pond and his 50-year-old wife fell in while trying to save him.
Both were Indonesian citizens working at the farm.
Papar district police chief Superintendent Heryan Mohd Tahir said police received information from a member of the public about the discovery at 11.56am.
He said a team from the Papar police station and the Fire and Rescue Department was sent to the scene.

"Initial investigations found that the male victim is believed to have slipped and fallen into the sewage pond, while his wife is believed to have tried to help him but also fell in," he said when contacted today.
Heryan said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation.
The bodies were sent to the forensic unit at Papar Hospital.
He said the case had been classified as a sudden death report.
0ad1a94093cc3feb: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the AI industry without its biggest champion and clouding the future of the chipmaker he built into an AI powerhouse.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the company said on Thursday. It named former Synopsys CEO and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chairman.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and is its fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61 per cent, will exit the board as well.
Nvidia shares fell more than 10 per cent in premarket trading, and weighed on the broader market.
Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to consider his ouster, a person familiar with the matter said, after reports earlier in the day that Huang also had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

Huang's exit plunges the US$4 trillion company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped bankroll by pouring Nvidia's swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry's biggest labs.
Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off.
The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang's push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump.
Trump said on Sunday that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country" and that the Nvidia chief had told him he had no idea the Chinese woman he had an affair with was a spy.

For years, Nvidia was best known to gamers chasing top-tier graphics. But its chips' ability to perform many calculations at once has made them the oil of the AI boom and a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate the technology. It also made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.

That turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who ask him to sign books, posters and sometimes even their bodies. Such is his pull that stocks moved at his mere mention of company names at events.

But scrutiny of his conduct has intensified in recent days after reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who US authorities have concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The two, who have been photographed together in Taiwan, Singapore and California, are not related.

Washington has also investigated Megaspeed, a coveted official Nvidia cloud partner with priority access to its chips, over suspicions it helped China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls, according to media reports. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

Earlier this month, Nvidia's board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.
The controversy escalated on Wednesday when the New York Times reported Jensen Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice-president of healthcare, who reported to him.
8e999fcfb73f509a: MELAKA: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim wants to hold further discussions with DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke over his resignation as transport minister.
Anwar said he had yet to receive Loke's resignation letter, despite the Seremban member of Parliament announcing his decision two days ago.
"I have not received Anthony Loke's resignation letter.
"If he wants to take a short break, that is fine. But if he wants to resign, we need to discuss the matter again," he said during Pakatan Harapan's grand finale rally here.
His statement was then followed shouts of agreement from supporters in the rally.

Loke had announced his immediate resignation following Tuesday's High Court decision allowing former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest.
Anwar, who is also PH chairman, defended Loke's performance as transport minister, saying there was no reason for an honest, trustworthy and committed minister to step down.
He said Loke had introduced various proposals, projects and programmes to improve public transport services and make daily travel easier for Malaysians, including taxi drivers.
"When I praise him, those from Pas and Umno question why Anwar is praising DAP or the Chinese.
"But when we appoint a minister, what matters is whether that minister is trustworthy, clean and hardworking.
"He has contributed many ideas, projects and programmes to make travelling easier for the people, including taxi drivers.
"Yet, people like him are being told to resign, while those who are problematic are being asked to stay. The world has turned upside down," he said.
Anwar also described Loke as a close friend and one of the Cabinet ministers who had consistently demonstrated a strong work ethic.
He said Loke's leadership had earned the respect of civil servants, including Malay officers serving in the Transport Ministry.
"He is among the ministers who work very hard and have many ideas to help ordinary Malaysians, particularly in transportation.
"I have spoken to Malay officers in his ministry, and he is well received by them," he said.
Anwar also criticised attempts to judge political leaders based on their race or party affiliation rather than their integrity and ability to serve.
He said Malaysia needed leaders from all communities who were honest, competent and committed to protecting the people's interests.

51bc80c0aaba060c: Students are demanding a just future for all
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of X video of the October 10, 2026 protest in Quito, Ecuador. Video by X user Elena Rodríguez. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.

Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador. Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.

However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center. The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:
Lo que pasa en Quito es impresionante:

Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse. Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa. @teleSURtv
— Elena Rodríguez Yánez (@ElenaDeQuito) October 10, 2026

What is happening in Quito is striking: Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse. Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.

With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents. Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
Structural failures driving youth mobilization

According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old. Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.

Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month. The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.

In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million. The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.
Slogans as the language of youth resistance

During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.

Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest. Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:

Estoy harta de tener que narrar, una y otra vez, las agresiones policiales contra la prensa. Hoy, mientras intentaba documentar la violencia con la que los agentes golpeaban a jóvenes manifestantes, recibí por la espalda un toletazo en la cabeza. Me di la vuelta, mostré mi micrófono de teleSUR para identificarme como periodista y la respuesta fue otro toletazo que terminó partiéndolo.

Los periodistas no queremos ser noticia. Yo no quiero ser protagonista de nada. Estoy en las calles para contar lo que ocurre, para documentar aquello que el poder muchas veces preferiría que nadie viera.

Y si creen que a punta de golpes van a conseguir que deje de registrar la brutalidad policial, que aparte mi micrófono o que me repliegue varias cuadras para ejercer el periodismo desde donde no incomode, se equivocan.
No somos los periodistas quienes debemos alejarnos de los hechos. Son los policías quienes deben dejar de agredir. El derecho a informar no se negocia a punta de tolete.
— Elena Rodríguez Yánez (@ElenaDeQuito) October 11, 2026

I am fed up with having to recount, time and again, police assaults against the press. Today, while attempting to document the violence with which officers were beating young protesters, I was struck on the back of the head with a baton. I turned around and held up my teleSUR microphone to identify myself as a journalist; the response was another blow from a baton, which ended up shattering it.

We journalists do not want to be the news. I have no desire to be the protagonist of anything. I am out on the streets to report on what is happening — to document things that those in power would often prefer no one to see.

And if they think that by using force — by raining down blows — they can make me stop recording police brutality, force me to put away my microphone, or push me back several blocks so that I might practice journalism from a place where I won’t cause any ‘inconvenience,’ they are sorely mistaken.
It is not the journalists who should step away from the events; it is the police who must stop the assaults. The right to report cannot be negotiated at the end of a baton.
Hatari Ulcuango, President of the Federation of Students of the Catholic University of Ecuador, warned in one of his speeches that these mobilizations were “just the beginning.”

On October 10, as young people occupied the streets with their marches and sit-ins, they also used art to make their voices heard, singing songs, playing musical instruments, wearing masks, and dressing up in costumes. In doing so, they demonstrated that together, they can be very strong and that violence is not needed to speak one’s mind.

The government responded by sending the authorities to quell the protests and repress the demonstrators. Denunciations of the outcomes of state violence — dozens of students suffocated, injured, and detained — quickly spread across social media. These young people promised, however, that as long as they go unheard and continue to be treated with the blunt coercion of the state, they will return to the streets and not falter.

The leading role of youth in the streets of Ecuador, pitted against the state’s capacity for violent repression, evidence not only the crisis of the social state and the consolidation of an exclusionary state, but also the historical role of young people as agents of political change.

The glass generation — the one society has tried to shield — is experiencing the contradictions of an economic and political system that excludes them, making their future increasingly uncertain, and they are doing something about it.
Written by Gina Yauri

b8969565bb0ca4f9: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future. Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available. As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit. I study how political and environmental risks affect international business. In my new book, “Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether. Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away. How climate risk affects foreign investment Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment. The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt. Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible. For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area. Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks. One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements. In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million. An aerial view shows scores of vehicles submerged at a flooded Honda factory in Thailand in November 2011. Paula Bronstein /Getty Images Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there. Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next. While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations. Who loses from investor avoidance? For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created. These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad. Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being. Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure. A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations. Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change. Lost opportunities for multinational companies When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company. Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities. For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt, while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel. These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change, which is likely scaring some companies away. Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries. Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets. Reducing investor avoidance There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries: Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed. International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya, Mozambique and Nigeria. Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many risk scores label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether. Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time. 9ac3f87d0b7ef077: State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years. That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40. The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it. Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “Today oligarchy has won.” As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality, I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second – or third or fourth – homes the very wealthy possess. Taxing the rich at the ballot box Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth. Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed. In Washington state, for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax. Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136, which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87, a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000. And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3. That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000. And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest. The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa. Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “millionaire protection cap.” People visit the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco, on Feb. 21, 2026, months before a ballot initiative that would have introduced such a measure failed to garner enough support. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures, rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged. In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets. And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate. In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes. Washington, D.C., Massachusetts and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023 and 2025, respectively. Taxing additional homes Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences. These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths. Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system, which took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates. New York City rolled out its “pied-à-terre tax” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence. Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences. And on Nov. 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target. However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks about the fiscal year 2027 budget in New York City on May 12, 2026. Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate. Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind. Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property and other assets – many of which are hard to estimate. The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock. Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. Calculating how much tax on real estate someone owes is easy for the authorities to do using annual municipal assessments. What might happen next? Despite Proposition 40’s defeat, it looks like Americans are generally open to taxing wealthy people more – at least when the states do it. In Illinois, where a billionaire governor, JB Pritzer, easily won a third term, another interesting ballot initiative prevailed. More than 75% of voters in Cook County, which includes Chicago and several of its suburbs, approved a nonbinding, advisory referendum asking if Illinois should adopt the “millionaire amendment for property tax relief and education.” It would levy a new surcharge of 3% on incomes over $1 million. While this win did not authorize a new tax, it revealed that support for one would be strong – at least in Chicago and Evanston. Even billionaire Bill Gates has said he believes a “billionaire’s tax” will be necessary. The question is: What kind? c98a5d34f1c61819: IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029.
Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations.
Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy.
Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits.

IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost.

The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. This tech was tested using Nighthawk r1 processors.

IBM previously outlined its goal of reaching reliable error correcting territory in 2029 with a quantum processor codenamed Starling. Now it intends for this to be the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 logical qubits.

This is an ambitious goal, considering fault-tolerant quantum technology always seems to be at least a decade away, despite numerous breakthroughs and technology introductions. However, some in the technology industry believe the odds on a working system are shortening, given the increased activity around making encryption ready with support for quantum-resistant algorithms.
Then again, a professor at the University of Auckland New Zealand famously claimed last year that quantum computers hadn't so far managed to factor any number greater than 21 without cheating.

IBM presented a framework for Starling in a 2025 paper outlining hardware to implement the improbably named bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes. These significantly reduce the number of physical qubits needed to store and process quantum information, compared to existing surface codes.

Using the architecture in the paper, Big Blue intends to assemble Starling from modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), allowing logic operations on the memory. The modules will have universal adapters letting them connect using l-couplers.
IBM is also preparing the way ahead by combining its quantum processors with classical high-performance compute (HPC) systems to research better quantum error correction.

Last week, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) in the US announced such a system, combining an IBM Quantum System Two with Nighthawk r2 quantum processors and Umbra, powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators.

IBM also has a partnership with Japan's RIKEN scientific research institute under which an IBM Quantum System Two has been integrated with the Fugaku Arm-based supercomputer, once the most powerful system in the world. ®
ae8b3856a7b09a61: KUALA LUMPUR: Police have busted 112 scam syndicates operating through call centres and detained 932 people in a nationwide operation conducted from Oct 19 to 31.
Bukit Aman Commercial Crime Investigation Department director Datuk Rusdi Mohd Isa said 153 raids were carried out during Op Magpie 01/2026, exceeding the initial target of 100.
He said police also conducted 650 proactive inspections of premises during the operation.
"Of the 932 people detained, 106 were Malaysians while 826 were foreigners. The arrests involved 796 men and 136 women.

"By nationality, Chinese nationals accounted for the highest number of arrests at 538, followed by Vietnam (93), Taiwan (40), Indonesia (36), Japan (21), Pakistan (18), Myanmar and the Philippines (14 each)," he told a press conference here today.

Rusdi said 106 of the 153 raids, or 69.28 per cent, were conducted at condominium residences, 34 at residential premises, eight at resorts or hotels and five at office buildings, shoplots and warehouses.

Initial analysis identified 136 records of scam modus operandi, with non-existent investment schemes and love scams accounting for 27 each, followed by phone scams (25), online gambling (16) and fake job offers (11).
The syndicates also targeted victims across national borders, with 130 of the 144 recorded target-country entries involving victims overseas and 14 in Malaysia.
China recorded the highest number of targets at 62, followed by the United States (12), Vietnam and Indonesia (seven each), and Japan and Hong Kong SAR (six each).

Police seized 2,058 mobile phones, 433 laptops or tablets, 161 computers or monitors, 112 routers or modems, 40 passports or visas and seven vehicles, along with various documents and equipment linked to the syndicates.
Cash amounting to RM102,635 was also seized.
Rusdi said 117 investigation papers were opened following the operation, with 70 still under investigation and 45 having reached the prosecution stage in court.
He said 809 of those arrested were identified as customer service personnel or operators, while another 70 were supervisors or team leaders.
Investigations were continuing to identify the syndicates' masterminds, operational coordinators and those responsible for managing their finances and providing facilities.
These efforts included digital forensic analysis, as well as examinations of communication records and financial transactions.
Police advised the public to beware of scams, protect their banking details and contact the NSRC on 997 if they suspected fraud.

79cfa1e1ce0f36d9: FRANKFURT: Germany's financial regulator said Thursday that it had fined Deutsche Bank €8 million over the botched integration of a smaller lender into its operations after a takeover.
It is the latest trouble for Germany's biggest lender stemming from its acquisition of Postbank, which began in 2010 and took several years.

The fine, levied by the regulator Bafin, consisted of two parts: €5.5 million for being too slow to respond to customer complaints, and €2.5 million for delays in transferring securities between banks.
Delays in transferring securities such as shares or bonds could have cost customers money since the investments are in limbo while they move between banks, stopping people from cashing out.

"Investment services enterprises must make and implement appropriate arrangements through adequate organisation in order to ensure the proper provision of investment services," Bafin said in a statement.
Orders to transfer securities accounts should be executed "without delay" and within three weeks at the latest, it said.
Deutsche Bank said it accepted Bafin's decision.
"We have thoroughly reviewed and resolved the issues associated with Postbank's IT migration to Deutsche Bank, which occurred several years ago," a spokesman said.
Deutsche Bank acquired a controlling stake in Postbank before building up its shares and merging Postbank into its own consumer bank in 2018.

In 2022 it began integrating their IT systems. Bafin took the rare step of appointing a special representative to Deutsche Bank in September 2023 to oversee the integration following customer complaints.
Deutsche Bank has also faced lawsuits from former Postbank shareholders who claimed the takeover shortchanged them.
The lender, based in Frankfurt, reached settlements with the investors in 2024.

45bb36293003f958: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments.

Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing.
ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015.

Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes.
Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected.

The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control.

Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console.

Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA.
Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity.
The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe.
ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access.

In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family.
It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit.
ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised.
The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself."

There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines.
That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed.
"We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote.

Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework.

Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk.

Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online.
Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed.

Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints."
And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

bc866c4bf647ff68: MANILA, Nov 12 — Global leaders are set to descend on Asia for a series of high-stakes meetings that will tackle everything from AI to trade to, potentially, nuclear disarmament.
AFP looks at a few of the key issues to watch for in the days ahead:
Three summits, five days

The 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) opens its final leaders’ summit of the year on Sunday in Manila, while French President Emmanuel Macron attends a Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh.
Focus then shifts north for the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) conference in Shenzhen.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to be a key figure at Apec, while India’s Narendra Modi will be attending the Asean meet.
US President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel to both.
Analysts told AFP that the bruising midterm election defeat Trump recently suffered will not appreciably change how the US president is perceived.
“I don’t think the region will see him as a lame duck,” Siew Mun Tang, former head of the Asean Studies Centre at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, told AFP.
“He has two more years. He can do a lot of things.”
Xi-Trump-Putin meet
The agenda for a proposed sit-down between China’s Xi Jinping, Trump and Putin may remain a mystery, but no meeting at the APEC conference will attract more attention.
While Putin has pushed for talks on Ukraine, Trump this week suggested the focus would be on denuclearisation and ending his faltering war in Iran.
Analysts who spoke to AFP cautioned expectations should be kept to a minimum.
“The symbolism... will account for a good portion of its substance,” the Brookings Institution’s Ryan Hass told AFP.
While he expects Xi and Putin to give Trump “a respectful hearing” on arms control, Hass said they will likely only “agree on broad principles without committing to any follow-on actions”.
Wang Wen, dean of Renmin University’s Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, agreed major outcomes were unlikely, calling it “a high probability that talks could end without a breakthrough”.
Separately, a meeting Trump once hoped for with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un appears dead in the water, with Pyongyang rejecting repeated overtures.
Eyeing AI safeguards
Artificial intelligence will be a hot topic at Apec, after Xi and Trump agreed in September to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.

Trump has repeatedly dismissed fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity. But despite the countries’ fierce tech rivalry, calls for cooperation are growing due to shared concerns regarding bioweapons and infrastructure hacking.
Xi in September said Washington and Beijing have a responsibility to “develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”.
Apec talks could build on the pair’s previous communication channel agreement, Stephen Wu, founder of Carthage Capital, told AFP.
“Both sides need an outcome, and a hotline is diplomacy’s cheapest: free to announce, free to ignore,” he said.

Meanwhile, a spying scandal enveloping Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, who was once widely expected to accompany Trump to Apec, threatens to cast a pall on AI discussions. US officials have accused him of sleeping with a woman they claim was working for Beijing.
Asean’s murky waters
In Manila, the Philippines’ year in the Asean chair looks set to come and go without fulfilling one of its top objectives: signing a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) with China.

The ongoing dispute over the waterway has cast a shadow over the bloc’s events all year. Philippine and Chinese sailors clashed a day before the start of a July summit, and a diplomatic row erupted at an October defence meeting.
One South-east Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations told AFP he did not see any agreement being reached in Manila.

228170cb0ac20593: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 12 — The Port Klang Free Zone (PKFZ) says it is prepared to provide relevant reports and facilitate regulatory audits amid concerns over the origin, authenticity and traceability of cooking oil products allegedly blended before being re-exported under Malaysian labels.

His response follows concerns raised last week by Maritime Network Sdn Bhd chief executive officer Datuk Seri R. Jeyenderan Ramasamy over the alleged blending of imported cooking oil with locally produced supplies before it is exported under Malaysian labels.

Jeyenderan said the alleged practice, which industry players have described as an oil “cocktail”, warranted closer scrutiny by the authorities, particularly over product origin, quality and food safety.

His remarks came after The Edge reported on Nov 4, citing industry sources, that imported palm oil was allegedly being blended with local supplies before being re-exported, potentially allowing foreign-origin oil to be marketed as Malaysian palm oil. Jeyenderan said an examination of cargo manifests and bills of lading had raised concerns over how the oil’s country of origin was declared and how its actual composition was verified after blending.

Jeyenderan, who has more than 30 years of experience in the maritime industry, said independent laboratory tests were needed to establish whether the imported oil and the final blended product met the required quality and food safety standards.

He also questioned whether oil samples were tested before the vessels carrying the cargo left Malaysian waters, claiming the vessels concerned were not equipped with specialised laboratory facilities or qualified chemists to carry out detailed analyses.
Jeyenderan said any possibility of contamination should be investigated through scientific testing rather than assumptions.
“If the oil is contaminated, what could be the impact on public health? Who is responsible for ensuring that the final product is safe for consumption?” he had asked previously.
He said international rules already set clear expectations on origin, testing and traceability.

Under the Codex Alimentarius, the international food standards adopted by the United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization and World Health Organization, the General Standard for the Labelling of Prepackaged Foods requires a food’s country of origin to be declared if leaving it out would mislead or deceive consumers.

“Codex only allows the origin to shift when processing changes the nature of the food. Simply mixing imported oil with Malaysian oil does not change its nature, so declaring the blend as wholly Malaysian may mislead buyers,” he was quoted saying.

On testing, he noted that international palm oil trade contracts under FOSFA International, including FOSFA Contract No. 81 issued jointly with the Palm Oil Refiners Association of Malaysia (PORAM), require independent analysis by qualified surveyors.

He also warned that Article 3 of the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which will apply to large operators from December 30, 2026, requires palm oil entering the EU to be traceable to the plots of land where it was produced.

He urged the authorities to clarify the procedures governing the import, blending, sampling, quality certification and re-export of cooking oil, including which agencies are responsible for monitoring each stage.

He said proper documentation and independent laboratory testing were essential to ensure that products exported from Malaysia complied with the required standards and that their country of origin was accurately declared.
He added that failing to address the concerns could affect consumer confidence and Malaysia’s reputation as a food exporter.

e163141dbe2b07ab: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants.
The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports.

There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux.
In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space.

What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published.

NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving. Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0, whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users.

Under the FreeBSD Core Team section, there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full:

Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient.

AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright.

Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent) and mandatory testing (39 percent).

Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool.

Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent, licensing and provenance (26 percent), and maintainability (21 percent). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing.

Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent), and transparency (78 percent) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy.
Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not.

Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection, and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on.

The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August. This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots.

With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®

555c0bc21f885b90: Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections.

Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory.

The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected.
"This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time."
You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems.

Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected.
And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load.
"It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service."
The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time."

Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with.
There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem.
According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012.

Microsoft, or rather the unfortunate souls responsible for administering their server products, has not had the best time of late. The October 2026 Windows Server update left some Exchange Servers wobbling until either a Registry edit was made or a fix was applied as part of the November update. ®
cfc6b95240187f97: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 12 — More than a century’s worth of knowledge and information on tropical forest biodiversity and science from the Forest Research Institute Malaysia (FRIM) is now accessible worldwide through its digital repository, the FRIM Research Depository (FRED).
