86393ff07c7e1bde: The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.
Originally published on Global Voices
Image courtesy HiiL

This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms. We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare. Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.

We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities. We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.

This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development. Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration. It is essential for economic and social infrastructure. Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability. With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.
The missing infrastructure of development

When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity. These investments matter. But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier? When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?

Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted. Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.

For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth. For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities. For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.

Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious. The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.

The scale of the problem is staggering. The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice. HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive. This is a crisis of development.
When injustice becomes insecurity
Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.

In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions. In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.

But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries. From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.

The consequences extend beyond those directly affected. When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates. When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state. And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge. Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms. At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence. We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.

This should fundamentally change how governments approach peacebuilding and security. Military and policing investments may respond to immediate threats, but accessible justice can help address grievances before they become security crises.
Justice should therefore be understood as preventive infrastructure, not merely a mechanism for responding to wrongdoing after it occurs.
What the evidence tells us

Fortunately, evidence from across HiiL’s global operations demonstrates how people-centred approaches are transforming the design and delivery of justice services. Rather than relying solely on formal courtrooms or conventional approaches to conflict resolution, community-led initiatives and alternative justice pathways are meeting people where their disputes actually occur.

In Kenya, research informed the Judiciary’s Social Transformation through Access to Justice (STAJ) Blueprint. The Alternative Justice Systems (AJS) centres in Kenya are resolving family, land and other disputes locally, thereby preserving community cohesion. In Ethiopia, government-led community justice centers bridge formal laws and customary traditions to deliver rapid, reconciliation-focused resolution. In Nigeria, pilot community justice centers and domestic violence one-stop shops in Imo and Ogun States provide scalable, data-driven dispute resolution. In Tunisia, digital platforms co-developed for employment disputes directly connect workers, employers, and inspectors to resolve conflicts before they escalate.
Instead of assuming what institutions need, the question is: What justice problems do people actually experience, and what would help resolve them fairly?

Through Justice Needs and Satisfaction (JNS) surveys, we gather data on everyday legal experiences rather than institutional outputs. The data consistently reveal a significant disconnect between supply and demand. In Tunisia, we found that nearly one in three adults experiences a legal problem annually, yet only a fraction reach formal courts. Similarly, research in Nigeria highlights widespread justice needs alongside heavy reliance on community and informal mechanisms. These insights expose the core limitation of traditional justice reform: expanding court capacity alone cannot solve the problem. People facing family, land, employment, or commercial disputes rarely seek lengthy litigation. They need solutions that are fair, accessible, affordable, and timely.

Similar approaches are yielding results. In Bangladesh, a government-led initiative has strengthened village courts, enabling rural communities to resolve minor disputes locally, more quickly and affordably. These courts resolved over 82 percent of reported cases in an average of 25 days, at an average cost of just USD 2.70 to users. In Canada, the Indigenous Justice Program supports community-based initiatives that involve Indigenous communities in designing and delivering culturally appropriate justice services, reflecting their needs and traditions. In Colombia, Houses of Justice bring together formal and informal justice services, providing communities with access to legal information, mediation and dispute resolution through integrated service centres. These examples illustrate how justice services can be brought closer to people and organised around different pathways to better respond to their needs.

This does not make courts obsolete; rather, it underscores that formal courts are only one component of a healthy justice ecosystem. To truly serve society, functional justice infrastructure must integrate formal institutions with trusted community mechanisms, mediation, legal support, and innovative services.
From justice reform to justice investment
If justice is infrastructure, we must fundamentally rethink how we finance, govern and deliver it.

First, governments must stop treating justice as the Ministry of Justice's exclusive responsibility. Economic planners, finance ministries, development institutions, businesses and peacebuilding organisations all have a stake in effective dispute resolution.

Second, justice investments must be guided by evidence about people's needs and outcomes. HiiL's Delivering Justice, Rigorously framework emphasises data, evidence-based practices, scalable services, enabling environments, and accountability.

Third, we must move beyond endless small-scale pilots towards financing solutions that demonstrate results and can reach entire populations. The Justice Financing Framework developed under the Justice Action Coalition offers important proposals for making people-centred justice services financially sustainable.

Finally, justice must become integral to development financing. International financial institutions and development partners should recognize that investments in agriculture, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, gender equality and peacebuilding depend partly on people’s ability to resolve disputes fairly and the credibility of the entire justice system. This is not an argument for diverting resources from development priorities. It is an argument for making those investments more effective and sustainable.
The foundation we cannot afford to ignore

The world faces intersecting crises of inequality, economic uncertainty, democratic distrust and violent conflict. Governments are searching for ways to build more resilient societies, yet one of the most important foundations of resilience remains chronically neglected.
Justice cannot continue to be treated as an institutional afterthought.

A society is not resilient simply because it has strong borders, modern highways or growing financial markets. It is resilient when people trust that grievances can be addressed fairly, rights can be protected, and conflicts can be resolved without violence.

The question is no longer whether we can afford to invest in people-centred justice. It is whether we can afford the economic, social and political consequences of failing to do so. This spotlight provides the argument for the justice case, evidence of what is working and a roadmap of what we must do to make justice work for our societies.
Udo Jude Ilo is the CEO of the Hague Institute for Innovation of Law.
Written by Guest Contributor

470fcb377593fa61: From Azam Mohd
Melaka’s new political understanding offers a revealing experiment: can parties cooperate without asking citizens to surrender the right to question them?

The BN–PAS arrangement, described as tafahum siyasi, is significant not because former rivals can share a platform, but because it tests whether political reconciliation can accommodate disagreement, scrutiny and plural representation.

On Oct 21, Barisan Nasional chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi announced an understanding under which BN would contest 21 of Melaka’s 28 constituencies, with seven allocated to PAS and its partners. By nomination day, however, the reported arrangement had changed: BN was contesting 23 seats and Perikatan Nasional five.
That revision matters. Negotiated formulas reflect political intentions; the actual ballot determines the choices voters face.

Melaka BN chief Ab Rauf Yusoh subsequently described PAS as a strategic partner and said the parties would coordinate their campaigns and share a manifesto. PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang has indicated that cooperation could extend beyond Melaka.
These statements point to an evolving political relationship, not a binding prediction about future governments or voter behaviour.

The more interesting issue is the meaning of understanding itself. "Tafahum" suggests a willingness to acknowledge differences while finding common ground. In a diverse federation, that can be constructive.
Consent of the governed
Yet political accommodation becomes fragile when leaders mistake agreement among elites for consent among citizens.
Malay political cooperation and Malaysia’s multiracial constitutional character need not conflict, but their compatibility must be demonstrated through policies and conduct.

Consider representation. BN includes component parties whose constituencies and organisational histories differ from those of PAS. A shared campaign must explain how minority interests, religious freedom, education and local economic concerns will be addressed, without assuming that a joint platform erases substantive disagreements.
Equally, voters sympathetic to PAS deserve clarity about which proposals remain party positions and which commitments have been accepted by all partners.

A joint manifesto creates an opportunity to answer those questions. It should identify priorities that can be implemented within state powers, distinguish them from federal responsibilities and specify how competing proposals would be reconciled.
Without such clarity, a manifesto risks becoming a catalogue of agreeable aspirations, with contradictions emerging only after polling.
State and federal ties

There is also a federal dimension. BN participates in the national unity government alongside Pakatan Harapan, while its cooperation in Melaka involves parties associated with the parliamentary opposition.
Such asymmetry is neither inherently unlawful nor unprecedented in coalition politics. Nevertheless, it complicates public understanding of accountability.

Leaders should explain whether state-level cooperation changes their federal commitments and where the boundaries between electoral partnerships and governmental responsibilities lie. This question cannot be answered through rhetoric about loyalty alone.

State administrations make decisions affecting land use, investment approvals, local infrastructure and public services. Business confidence depends less on displays of unity than on whether policies remain clear and decisions can be challenged through established institutions.
Keeping spotlight on
There is no available evidence to establish that this electoral understanding has already changed investment outcomes; that would require separate analysis.

For Pakatan Harapan and other competitors, the appropriate response is substantive scrutiny rather than assuming that cooperation proves ideological inconsistency. Parties routinely negotiate across previous divisions.

What matters democratically is whether voters receive accurate explanations of those negotiations and meaningful policy alternatives. Criticism should focus on documented commitments, not speculative claims about hidden intentions.

The outcome of the Nov 14 election will reveal the choices made by voters, but not necessarily why each choice was made. Turnout, candidates, local grievances and broader party loyalties all interact. Claims that a new Malay consensus has emerged require evidence beyond leadership appearances and seat allocations.
Three questions
Electoral results should be interpreted cautiously, especially when several political relationships are changing simultaneously.

My assessment is that Melaka’s experiment should be measured against three questions: Are shared commitments sufficiently precise to be evaluated? Can participating parties disagree openly without paralysing the administration? And will citizens outside the parties’ principal constituencies enjoy equal access to representation and public services?
That obligation extends to opposition scrutiny, legislative debate and the independence of public institutions.
Political understanding acquires democratic meaning when it protects disagreement as well as cooperation.
Beyond Melaka, BN and PAS face a continuing choice between treating tafahum siyasi as a temporary arrangement among leaders and developing transparent principles that voters can examine.
Malaysia’s political maturity depends not on eliminating differences, but on making cooperation accountable to everyone affected by it.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
1b1e59572933e14d: Citizens in Gabon went 248 days without access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube
Originally published on Global Voices
Image of a smartphone showing the Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, and Messenger apps. Screenshot from the DW Afrique YouTube channel.

After more than eight months of government blockage, Gabon has restored its social media access. But it has come at a cost. This reinstatement comes with a tighter regulatory framework and an unprecedented cooperation between the government and various tech giants, raising serious concerns about freedom of expression and privacy.

On February 17, 2026, Gabon’s media regulator, the High Communication Authority (HAC), suspended major social media networks, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, “until further notice.” According to the regulator, quoted in the daily newspaper L’Essentiel, this measure targeted not only content “undermining national security” but also content involving defamation, cyberbullying, hate speech, and threats to social cohesion.

At first, the suspension had no real impact, with presidential spokesperson Jennyfer Mélodie Sambat claiming it would solely target Meta platforms. However, according to Gabon Media Time, several influencers, content creators, and citizens later experienced access disruptions on YouTube and TikTok, sometimes rendering connections impossible without a bypass tool, such as a virtual private network (VPN).

The global data platform Internet Society Pulse confirmed this observation, revealing major anomalies for Meta, Telegram, TikTok, and YouTube, but not X (formerly Twitter). The online news portal Le360 Afrique consequently reported a surge in VPN usage in the months that followed.
For 248 days, more than 1.84 million individuals, or 71.9 percent of the country’s population of over 2.5 million, were denied regular access to some of the world’s most popular digital platforms.

On October 24, 2026, the HAC lifted this suspension, with Africanews stressing that this ruling didn’t necessarily mean a return to business as usual. It, therefore, remains to be seen whether Gabon, where Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema has been president since September 2023, will restore digital freedoms or establish a new state-controlled online model instead.
From bypassing the suspension to tighter regulatory frameworks

A new legal framework, enacted on February 26, 2026, underpins this reinstatement. According to Gabon Media Time, Ordinance No. 0011/PR/2026 establishes a regulatory framework for digital platform usage, while Ordinance No. 0013/PR/2026 amends the HAC Reorganization Act.

The HAC also invokes a law, enacted on October 5, that ratifies the social media ordinance and establishes a regulatory framework for AI-generated and AI-amplified content, according to reporting by Gabon Review.

What’s more, available data shows that these regulations have introduced joint liability for those who create and share illegal content and require all social media users to provide personal identification information. Purported as tools to combat abuse, these regulations have raised serious concerns about anonymity, personal data protection, and their stifling effect on public debate.
In a country where criticizing public institutions is politically sensitive, the threat of prosecution for posting online could discourage users from expressing dissent.

The issue here isn’t whether the state should combat cyberbullying, disinformation, or hate speech, but rather how. While these are valid concerns, the real worry is whether its measures are transparent, proportionate, and subject to independent scrutiny.
Tech giants enter the regulatory mix

The most decisive development in this saga was undoubtedly the unprecedented cooperation between the government and Big Tech companies. On July 13, 2026, after a meeting at the AI for Good/WSIS summit in Geneva, Gabonese Minister of Digital Economy Mark-Alexandre Doumba announced an agreement with TikTok. Both parties signed a 12-month cooperation agreement, ensuring the platform’s compliance with Gabon’s new regulatory framework.
At the meeting, TikTok presented its Q1 2026 content moderation results, revealing that it had removed more than 23,500 pieces of sensitive content in Gabon.

Meanwhile, the HAC confirmed that it had established an “active cooperation” with TikTok, Meta, and YouTube to “improve content moderation.” The regulator added that, during the suspension, it also held direct discussions with these companies. However, neither the technical details of these exchanges nor the practical operation of the authorities’ reporting tools has been specified.
Find the HAC spokesperson’s full statement here:

These agreements reflect tech companies’ growing influence in digital platform governance. These platforms are also no longer satisfied with merely hosting exchanges between their users; they now shape decisions about what content remains accessible and what does not.

For governments, partnerships with digital platforms provide a direct channel to deal with content they consider harmful, illegal, or threatening to their regime. For tech companies, complying with the state’s requests and distinguishing legitimate moderation from politically motivated censorship poses a significant challenge.
Cooperation is no substitute for transparency
Working alongside digital platforms isn’t inherently problematic. Tech companies ultimately have a responsibility to deal with credible threats, protect vulnerable users, and enforce their own rules.

However, problems arise when the state has direct access to reporting mechanisms — particularly if the public remains unaware of these partnerships. What criteria determine which content is flagged? How are HAC requests processed? Can users challenge a post removal? Are there any safeguards to protect journalists, activists, and government critics?

The line between harmful content and legitimate political expression is often blurred. Without clear procedures, independent monitoring, and an appeals process, critics say these measures risk becoming tools of influence over public debate.

The situation in Gabon represents a much broader trend. As various African states tighten their grip on digital platforms, tech companies face escalating pressure to comply with new national regulations to maintain key market access. The balance of power between governments and tech giants has ultimately become a defining factor in the future of digital rights.
Beyond Gabon: Who is accountable for digital freedom?
Restoring social media access was imperative for Gabonese citizens, journalists, businesspeople, and content creators alike, all of whom suffered under this suspension.

However, access alone doesn’t guarantee freedom. The real test will be whether internet users can participate in online discussions, criticize public policy, and share information without fear of arbitrary sanctions or disproportionate restrictions.

It also depends on Meta, TikTok, and YouTube demonstrating how their cooperation with the Gabonese government complies with international human rights standards, especially freedom of expression, privacy, and access to information.

The current situation in Gabon illustrates how authoritarian control over the digital sphere evolves. Restrictions don’t necessarily end when platform accessibility is restored. Instead, they become regulatory frameworks, personal identification requirements, and tighter government cooperation with private tech companies.

The challenge, therefore, isn’t just about reconnecting citizens to social media, but also about ensuring the digital spaces they return to remain open to criticism, independent information, and public debate.
Although tech giants can negotiate conditions allowing citizens to regain access to digital platforms, they must also ensure those conditions don’t compromise their fundamental freedoms.

60f80913d48f881c: One could be forgiven for thinking the world is hurtling towards an apocalyptic end and that humanity is about to reenact Mad Max, complete with spiked leather jackets and tribal warfare over the last remaining can of baked beans.

This is because more than 30 countries have recently issued “be prepared” warnings, sending preppers – those who prepare for the day when the grid goes down, the shelves go empty, and the world as we know it ends – into another frenzy of stockpiling and repetitions of “I knew it was coming”.

The world has become more dangerous—or at least appears so. With never-ending global conflicts, meteorological tantrums, and the instant, vibrating hum of social media algorithms pinging our dopamine receptors twenty-four hours a day, crises are no longer experienced; they are simulated in our heads before they even happen.

And social media amplifies crises in ways the older generation —who blissfully survived on slow-moving broadsheets and evening radio—never experienced. What once trickled down as boring administrative updates now floods our phones in real-time, inducing a collective, low-grade heart flutter.

When roughly 30 nations update their civil resilience playbooks in the same calendar window, algorithms do what they do best: they hallucinate a conspiracy. Social media sharing stitches these independent notices together into a terrifying mosaic of a coordinated global doom narrative.
Some viral headlines scream that something’s going terribly wrong; others claim governments are secretly preparing us for war and not telling us the whole story.
The world has always had its dangers; the difference today is that mechanisms for broadcasting anxiety have become infinitely more efficient.
The reality, as is so often the case, is wonderfully, boringly mundane.
To understand the October 2026 wave, we must separate routine government weather chores from modern media panic.

Take Malaysia. In late October 2026, the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) issued its thoroughly familiar seasonal reminder: citizens should “stock up sensibly” ahead of the northeast monsoon. The call was a practical, sober reminder to prepare for seasonal flooding—a ritual practiced faithfully every year since the 1990s across Southeast Asia.

Yet, this routine tropical memo collided on the calendar with a broader occidental wave, most notably the UK’s newly minted “Be Ready” campaign, launched under Prime Minister Andy Burnham to encourage multi-year resilience against generic short-term infrastructure glitches or cyberattacks.

When a seasonal flood warning in Kuala Lumpur and an all-hazards resilience campaign in London drop in the same fortnight, and more than 30 nations issue similar advisories, digital platforms turn it into a blockbuster movie trailer.
This happened despite every official source emphasizing the same thing: the advice was voluntary, gradual, and completely unrelated to any looming apocalypse.
So why are governments suddenly nagging us about emergency kits? Is the world ending? No. But our infrastructure has quietly evolved.

In the old days, if a local transformer blew out,your neighbourhood went dark, and we used a candle until power was restored. Today, because our banking, logistics, communications, and heating rely on digital infrastructure and interconnected power grids, a minor disruption cascades instantly across sectors.
Governments aren't warning us because war is at the door; they are doing it because hyper-connected societies are inherently fragile to short-term hiccups.

Predictably, human nature did what it always does. In the UK, Malaysia and elsewhere, some took to social media to urge people to stock up on food or actually cleared supermarket shelves of certain items, proving once again that panic is far more infectious than any virus.

They chose to ignore the advice to buy gradually and not panic. So much so that Nadma director-general Meor Ismail Meor Akim felt it necessary to issue a statement saying: “We should avoid such panic-buying messages. Sometimes, panic buying creates another problem, not a northeast monsoon disaster, but a shortage of goods instead. Just buy according to your needs.”
This brings us to the most important distinction of all: the gap between selfish hoarding and civic self-reliance.
When a government tells us to store a 72-hour buffer of water, a torch, and non-perishables, it isn't inviting us to join a doomsday cult. It is an exercise in decentralised pragmatism.

If households are self-sufficient for three days during a sudden power outage or flash flood, it keeps arterial roads uncluttered and emergency phone lines open for people facing actual life-and-death medical emergencies. And for other such emergencies.

An emergency kit isn't a survivalist fetish; it’s an act of civic hygiene. It’s the modern equivalent of bringing your own bucket to a neighbourhood fire instead of standing in the street screaming that the town is cursed.

Ultimately, these advisories don't signal a descent into martial law or long-term catastrophes. They reflect the tedious, necessary business of living in a complex world. Just as learning fire safety or getting vaccinated became the unremarked background noise of twentieth-century life, digital-age resilience is simply the new baseline of modern citizenship.
How should we respond?
We would do well to ignore the merchants of panic—whether they write viral social media threads or sensationalist headlines—and consult sober official sources instead.

By preparing quietly, rationally, and without melodrama, we insulate ourselves against minor tempests while preserving the sanity of the commonwealth at large. After all, if the world truly is coming to an end, panicking in the supermarket checkout queue is a singularly undignified way to greet the final curtain.

e0f47e1eef07df75: I drove to Seremban from my humble abode recently and covered 106km, if one rather disreputable GPS app is to be believed. My journey began on the northern route of the North-South Expressway which is numbered E1 as well as AH2 (for Asian Highway 2). If you've ever wondered what those small signs meant, you’re welcome!

At Sungai Buloh, the E1 morphed into the New Klang Valley Expressway (NKVE) and a new Asian Highway designation, the AH141. Later, I was back on some federal and city roads for a while before I rejoined the NSE at Sungai Besi on its southern route, numbered E2. Later at Bangi the E2 became the AH2 again.

On my return journey, the said disreputable GPS app took me through some quaint Seremban back roads where life appeared slower and I was reminded of the Penang I knew from many decades ago. I was then guided out of town and on to another expressway, the E21 or Lekas, yet another fancy acronym in this never-ending battle amongst toll highway concessionaires to pick the coolest name possible for their particular concession.

Lekas – fast in Malay – quickly took me away from Seremban’s charming old town and countryside and handed me over to the E18, the Kajang Dispersal Link Expressway or SILK, which is somehow a Malay acronym because apparently KDLE doesn’t sound very exciting. SILK smoothly took me onto the E27, the East Klang Valley Expressway, or EKVE, which probably means something cool in some language I’m not au fait with, perhaps French.

The E27 took me to the E19, the Sungai Besi Ulu Kelang Elevated Expressway (SUKE), which deposited me on the E33, the Duta Ulu Klang Expressway (DUKE), which also happens to be part of the AH141. I went from SUKE to DUKE, or from happiness to sadness, if your Malay is au courant.

Sad indeed, as there I was in a small sedan and not my usual thirsty but spacious old 4x4, which consumes a litre of petrol just coughing itself to a start. My back and knees and ego hurt while I looked up to other motorists rather than down on them – a rather unnerving and humbling experience indeed.

I duked my way out of the late afternoon traffic on the E33 back to the recently-traversed E1 incorporating the NKVE, and made my way home, which remains a humble abode regardless of how many French words I throw out to the hoi polloi in telling this story.
At this point, you’re probably close to screaming “Is there a point to all this?” Yes, there indeed are some points I’m trying to make, so hold on to your pantalons, dear readers.

I’ve driven on almost all major roads and highways and byways in Malaysia, especially on the peninsular side. But it appears Malaysia’s appetite for building toll expressways far exceeds my capacity to drive on each and every one of them.

I should have paid more attention when rich people objected to yet another expressway running through their neighbourhood and bringing down property values. Or when the conservation-minded people shouted about yet another toll highway cutting through some pristine nature preserve. All these mean yet another highway with a cute name and many toll booths is being born.

I’ve seen expressways that seem to just hang in the sky, and had I chosen the E12 Akleh elevated highway instead of the E33, or better still, taken the E12 and then still went on to the E33, my story would’ve been more fantastique and my knees more swollen.

Had fate and my GPS app taken me on slightly different routes, I could very easily have added the E6 Elite, the E20 Maju and maybe even the E38 SMART Tunnel to the list of highway concessions I helped enrich. With a few more diversions I could’ve also added the E31 DASH, the E23 SPRINT, the E6 Kesas, possibly the E11 LDP and the E13 LKSA, and closer to home, the E25 Latar and perhaps even the E35 GCE.

These are not all. Elsewhere and not quite taking me to Seremban are the E7 CKE, the E8 ECE, the E9 Besraya, the E10 NPE, the E26 SKVE, the E29 SPDH, the E30 NNKSB and the E37 LKS. These are all within the Kuala Lumpur-Seremban metropolitan area, and many of you probably drive on them regularly without realising how magnificent, intricate and widespread our toll highway network is.
But a blessing can also be a curse. More on that when the journey continues.

bda5de5f5ee664c9: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

2dcde4b665668871: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.

Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge.

An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).
a5443af359df1d11: They are learning how to be drivers of change locally
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the Voices of Democracy project in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photo by beYOUnd. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information. At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.

Despite the war, people can still submit petitions, participate in public consultations, or advocate for their needs online, but there is a lack of awareness about such opportunities. Furthermore, vulnerable groups — including displaced persons, minorities, and rural communities — know they have a voice, but struggle to find it.

In 2026, the local non-governmental organization beYOUnd implemented a project to help youth from vulnerable groups acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to find their voices in this new era of digital democracy. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Yevheniia Holovenko, the chairwoman of beYOUnd, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Yevheniia Holovenko (YH): beYOUnd is a youth-led NGO based in Ukraine, registered in October 2025, though we’ve worked as a team long before that. Our mission is to increase the involvement of vulnerable youth, especially internally displaced people and young people facing difficult social and economic circumstances, in integration, self-realization, and civic life.

Our name reflects our philosophy: it starts with you; it goes beyond! Our team is largely made up of young people who’ve lived through the same challenges as the youth we work with, which shapes how we approach everything we do.

We joined the Digital Sparks initiative because digital democracy and civic space are exactly where Ukrainian youth need support right now. Safe, informed participation online is inseparable from resilience during war, and it matched our mission perfectly.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

YH: The war has pushed many young Ukrainians, especially internally displaced persons (IDPs), into digital spaces to stay connected, informed, and civically active, often without the tools to do so safely.
We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything.

We wanted to close this gap by developing practical digital safety and civic participation skills in displaced and marginalized youth. We wanted to give them an opportunity to share ideas on how to increase awareness of digital democracy with the involvement of young people in Ukraine.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
YH: Within the project “Voices of Democracy in the Digital Era,” we ran an awareness campaign covering digital security, e-participation, and disinformation, which reached over 8,500 views.
On the education side, we delivered three webinars and three workshops on digital democracy, media literacy, civic action planning, and cybersecurity, engaging over a hundred participants.

We also organized an offline networking event in the capital, Kyiv, bringing 27 participants together in person to connect around these same topics, and build on the online learning with real, face-to-face relationships and exchange.
Together, these activities, which combined online reach with in-person community building, gave young people both the knowledge and the network to act on this newly acquired knowledge.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

YH: “Voices of Democracy” reshaped how our beneficiaries see their own place in their community. As one participant shared, “I discovered new digital tools I can use to engage with my community and take part in important decisions.”
Others said the most valuable part was learning how to protect their personal data and use digital services safely in everyday life.
Several highlighted finally understanding the difference between advocacy and broader civic action, and how to build a real plan for their own initiative — skills that came alive through teamwork.

As another participant put it, “I learned to define a problem, trace its causes, and plan real steps to solve it — and I understood better what advocacy is and how it can drive positive change in a community.”
For many, this changed how they see their own ability to influence change locally.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

YH: Leading this project deepened our understanding of how closely digital safety and democratic participation are linked. You can’t meaningfully engage young people in civic life online without first equipping them to navigate that space securely.
Working alongside experts in digital security and civic engagement broadened our grasp of practical tools we now use, and how we think about beYOUnd’s programming.

It also pushed us to see capacity-building more structurally: not just what we teach beneficiaries, but how we build our own organizational resilience for the long term, not just on a project-by-project basis.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

YH: The biggest lesson was that combining practical, hands-on content with real interaction (webinars, workshops, and offline networking) worked far better than any one format alone. Participants didn’t just absorb information; they built relationships and confidence to act on it, especially through the in-person exchange in Kyiv.
We also learned how much value there is in simple, clear, practical content. Participants consistently said what stuck with them most was information they could immediately use, not abstract theory.
Finally, working through capacity-building for our own team alongside the project reminded us that organizational resilience matters just as much as the skills we pass on to beneficiaries.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

YH: We plan to keep the digital tools, advocacy frameworks, and civic action planning skills from this project embedded in how we design future programs for youth. This isn’t a one-off topic, but now a standing part of our work.
The connections built through the Kyiv networking event are something we want to keep nurturing, turning one-time contacts into an ongoing community.

On the organizational side, we’re applying what we’ve built around resilience and long-term capacity to strengthen beYOUnd as we grow, so we’re better equipped to run projects like this and bigger ones going forward.

[00:05:56] BARRY RITHOLTZ: They ended up doing pretty okay during the financial crisis. Some companies did a little better, a lot did a whole lot worse. But it was definitely a lot of stress. What was it like starting your career right in the middle of that storm?

And I’m pretty sure I was kept ’cause I was just very cheap, right? ’Cause I was really entry level coming out of business school. And the stress levels were incredibly high. And I remember Lloyd Blankfein, who was CEO at the time—he was actually very good about sending out frequent voicemails. It was a big voicemail culture. And you’d see your phone bleeping, your desk phone bleeping, and his voicemails would start: “This is Lloyd with an update.” And those would come around pretty frequently. And I learned weekly—
[00:06:49] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Daily?

[00:06:49] ANN BERRY: Sometimes several times a week, particularly if the headlines were rolling, just to clarify what was going on. And I will say I was very impressed that, while I’m sure the senior folks were incredibly stressed, both personally and professionally, the people I worked with did a pretty good job of emanating at least a feeling of calm—that things will be all right. And there was always a question around which of the banks would survive. I remember the moment that Goldman became a bank holding company. Lots of people who’d grown up at Goldman weren’t particularly excited about that. But there was a sense that Goldman would figure it out. So I was lucky to be there at that time. And I learned a lot, by the way, from my portfolio companies, the businesses, ’cause I was in private equity at Goldman in ’08—the things you have to do to help companies survive. And I’ll just plant one, ’cause it became very important later in my career, Barry: I inherited an oil field services company—
[00:07:48] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Meaning someone else at the firm was responsible?

[00:07:51] ANN BERRY: They had made the investment. And I joined the team, so I was supporting a senior person. And this business had struggled, as many did; it had a lot of leverage on it. But it had the wherewithal to pull down on its revolver to max out its cash balance, right, as they could see the problems were coming. And I was tasked with figuring out where to cut cost, how to reserve that cash. It was very operational. It was unusual for private equity. [00:08:32] BARRY RITHOLTZ: People don’t realize, during these big crises, it’s a tremendous learning opportunity—
[00:08:36] ANN BERRY: Fabulous learning experience.

[00:08:37] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Amongst the wreckage and the tragedies, there’s a lot of opportunity for learning, for growth. [00:09:08] ANN BERRY: Right. So post–business school, I spent about nine-ish years at Goldman—I think it was nine years at Goldman—in New York, in the merchant bank, as it was then called, doing private equity investing. [00:10:33] ANN BERRY: Well, you don’t have brand recognition. [00:14:20] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Not just Fox, but you eventually start doing Bloomberg—
[00:14:23] ANN BERRY: CNBC, Bloomberg—
[00:14:25] BARRY RITHOLTZ: CNN. The whole run. How did you end up at Jimmy Kimmel’s media platform, Wheelhouse?

[00:14:32] ANN BERRY: So after Cornell Capital—well, there’s a chapter within Cornell Capital which meant a lot to me. I became the CEO of one of the largest portfolio companies in their portfolio, called PureStar. And—
[00:14:44] BARRY RITHOLTZ: That was during the pandemic, right?

[00:14:53] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Through—
[00:14:54] ANN BERRY: The pandemic, through the lockdown.
[00:14:55] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And this is the hospitality company where you’re working with hotels and—
[00:14:59] ANN BERRY: Re—
[00:14:59] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Restaurants, which are all suffering tremendously, right, when their guests can’t show up. Well, let me—

[00:15:05] ANN BERRY: Tell you a story for how it became clear things were going to get tough for that business, which by the way is doing incredibly well today. I always remember this. It was early 2020, and Vegas had just had CES, the Consumer Electronics Show—big deal. Vegas, an important market in hospitality. And I was out there, and I’ll always remember this, Barry: I was sitting in the office, and several generations of one family, who had grown up in this business starting at the age of seventeen, came to me, and they said, “Ann, something’s going on. [00:15:48] ANN BERRY: This is February 2020. But much earlier than when we had the lockdowns come and the shutdowns come. 0f696e8c856711df: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark.

DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5.

DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate.
68f66ac0cbd7169a: It was a fun few weeks while it lasted. People using both Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex to do AI-powered “reverse-engineering” or decompiling are now hitting guardrails or having their accounts limited while trying to do things like unbrick their internet-of-things devices or remove surveillance ads from their smart TVs.

Several people have reported triggering “safety checks” in Claude Code that prevented them from doing AI-powered reverse engineering; a highly upvoted Reddit post in r/ClaudeCode reads “The Dream is dead. Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is not likely to work with Claude.” A thread in the Reverse Engineer Anything Discord from last week reads, “Claude is refusing to decompile anything,” with multiple users responding saying they have hit similar walls. And X user log4j, who used OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs, reported having their OpenAI account banned for violating its rules on “cyber abuse.” Other users said they asked Codex to reverse engineer hardware or their own code now say they have either been warned by the company or had their accounts restricted. A project called Decomp.wtf that made it easier to reverse engineer software and games has also shut down in recent days.

As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior.

The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most.

Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, tweeted that people are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted.

But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails.
4ac67656f256b571: From Jamaluddin Aziz

The announcement that the Islamic development department (Jakim) and central committee for applications for filming and performances by foreign artistes (Puspal) are investigating alleged elements of ritualistic worship at The Weeknd’s recent concerts at the Bukit Jalil national stadium highlights a recurring cultural tension in Malaysia.
As a critical media scholar, I view this controversy not merely as a clash over entertainment guidelines, but as a textbook case of “context collapse”.

Coined by media researcher Danah Boyd and further theorised with Alice Marwick in their seminal 2011 study in New Media & Society (“I tweet honestly, I tweet passionately: Twitter users, context collapse, and the imagined audience”), context collapse occurs when digital platforms flatten multiple, distinct audiences into a single space.

When content created for one specific cultural or artistic environment is stripped of its original framing and judged within an entirely different moral or ideological context, modern pop theatrics are easily misread as literal religious devotion.

To understand how context shapes interpretation, one need only compare The Weeknd’s Nov 4 and 5 shows with another massive event held at the exact same stadium just three weeks earlier: Konsert Tradisional Gema Bumantara by Biduanita Negara Siti Nurhaliza.
Both concerts drew tens of thousands of devoted fans who sang every lyric in unison and cheered wildly for their favourite performer.
Yet, the public and institutional reactions to these two sold-out spectacles could not have been more different.

In modern pop culture, intense audience enthusiasm is often loosely referred to as “fan worship”. Historically, words like “fan” (from the Latin fanaticus, meaning temple frenzy) and “icon” (from the Greek eikōn, meaning sacred image) do share etymological roots in ancient religious practice.
Today, however, these terms describe secular cultural admiration. When fans cheer at a stadium, they are participating in collective musical enjoyment, not a spiritual ritual.

Viewing both Bukit Jalil concerts through a critical media lens reveals three key dynamics driving these divergent reactions. First is the mechanics of context collapse. Critics of The Weeknd’s concert pointed to short social media clips showing a towering golden female robot sculpture and dancers in red hooded robes as evidence of pagan or machine-worship rituals.

As Marwick and Boyd’s framework demonstrates, when these visuals are detached from the full two-hour concert narrative and circulated online to audiences unfamiliar with Western pop-art tropes, context collapses.
Stripped of their theatrical framing, a futuristic sculpture by Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama meant to critique the hollowness of fame and materialism is flattened into a literal religious idol.

Second is embedded cultural context. In contrast, Siti’s concert operated within a shared, deeply understood local framework. Utilising classical floral visuals and orchestral staging without human statues, her performance aligned seamlessly with Malaysian cultural and religious norms.

Because audiences and regulators immediately understood the context of Irama Malaysia heritage, the collective euphoria in the stadium was celebrated as patriotic pride rather than scrutinised as spiritual misdirection.

At most, conservative critiques of such local shows rarely go beyond general moral cautions against lagha (worldly distraction or frivolous amusement), a far cry from the theological panic of syirik (idolatry) projected onto The Weeknd’s unfamiliar pop symbolism.
Third is audience literacy and intent. Context collapse assumes that audiences are passive consumers who absorb imagery literally.
In reality, modern concertgoers possess high media literacy. Tens of thousands of Malaysians attended The Weeknd’s show to experience Grammy-winning music and dystopian sci-fi stagecraft.

Treating theatrical props as acts of syirik (idolatry) ignores the crucial distinction between artistic metaphor and religious intent (niat), unfairly questioning the faith and intelligence of ordinary Malaysian fans.
Puspal plays an essential role in ensuring that international performances respect Malaysia’s laws and social harmony.
However, effective regulation in the digital age requires media literacy and a resistance to reactionary interpretations born out of viral, out-of-context video clips.

If Malaysia wishes to remain a premier destination for global live entertainment, bringing vital economic and tourism benefits to Kuala Lumpur, authorities must evaluate performances within their full artistic context.
Distinguishing between pop-culture symbolism and actual religious worship is not just good cultural policy; it is essential for fair and rational governance.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
08367870b5ce119e: A series of tax cuts since President George W. Bush's 2001 legislation have helped push the national debt to US$32 trillion. AP Photo/Ron EdmondsDemocrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy. Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living. Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt. The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found. The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper, the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts. I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing. It’s all relative Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise. U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen. At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan think tank, noted. President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth. Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts. Costly extensions While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025. But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts. The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034. Why deficits and economic growth matter so much A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not. If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well. This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office. In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats. It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century. Hinckley Jones-Sanpei does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
1b207d990733aaf1: Nearby stores might not actually win out with extra shoppers if a Walmart shutters. Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty ImagesShoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business. Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants. Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes. A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area. This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough. Developers often place an anchor store in a bigger retail center to attract more foot traffic overall, which in turn goes to other stores. David Cooper/Toronto Star via Getty Images What happened after a Walmart closed We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open. We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes. That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared. In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally. Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand. Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales. Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed. These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure. Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores. That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits. For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s. Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area. Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic.
